Some ten minutes afterwards the tea-bell sounded, and when Virginia failed to appear, Mrs. Otis sent a footman upstairs to summon her. Presently he returned with the news that Miss Virginia was nowhere to be found. Since she usually went into the garden each evening to gather flowers for the dinner-table, her mother felt no alarm at first. But when the clock struck six and Virginia still did not come, Mrs. Otis grew seriously disturbed. She sent the boys to search outside, while she and Mr. Otis examined every room of the house. At half past six the boys returned, having discovered no sign of their sister anywhere. All were now intensely agitated and quite at a loss, when Mr. Otis recollected that a few days earlier he had allowed a company of gypsies to pitch their camp in the park. He therefore set out immediately for Blackfell Hollow, where he knew the camp lay, taking his eldest son and two farm-servants. The little Duke of Cheshire, beside himself with anxiety, pleaded earnestly to accompany them; but Mr. Otis refused, fearing some encounter might lead to a fight. When he reached the place, however, the gypsies had departed. Their leaving had plainly been somewhat hurried, for their fire still burned and several plates remained upon the grass. Sending Washington and the two men to search the surrounding country, he hurried back to the house and telegraphed every police inspector in the county, asking them to watch for a young girl carried off by tramps or gypsies. Next he ordered his horse brought round. Having insisted that his wife and the three boys sit down to dinner, he rode away along the Ascot Road, attended by a groom. They had scarcely covered two miles before he heard someone galloping behind them. Turning, he saw the little Duke overtaking him on his pony, bareheaded and with a deeply flushed face. ‘I’m dreadfully sorry, Mr. Otis,’ the boy said breathlessly, ‘but I simply can’t eat dinner while Virginia is missing. Please don’t be cross with me. If you had allowed us to get engaged last year, none of this trouble would have happened. You aren’t going to send me home, are you? I can’t go back! I won’t!’

The Minister could not refrain from smiling at the handsome young rascal, and Virginia’s devoted champion moved him considerably. Bending from his saddle, he gave the boy a friendly pat on the shoulders and said, ‘Well, Cecil, since you refuse to return, I suppose you must accompany me. But we shall have to find you a hat at Ascot.’

In the middle of this opening I noticed a white spot, but at first I could not tell what it was. I adjusted the telescope’s focus and looked again. This time I could see that it was a human skull.

“After that discovery I felt confident enough to believe I had solved the puzzle. The words ‘main branch, seventh limb, east side’ could only describe the skull’s position in the tree. And in a search for buried treasure, ‘shoot from the left eye of the death’s head’ could also mean only one thing. I understood that I was meant to drop a bullet through the skull’s left eye. A straight line drawn from the nearest point of the trunk through ‘the shot’—the place where the bullet landed—and then continued for fifty feet would lead to a precise spot. I thought it at least possible that something valuable lay buried beneath it.”

“That is all extremely clear,” I said. “The plan is clever, but also simple and definite. What happened after you left the Bishop’s Hotel?”

“Well, once I had carefully noted the direction of the tree, I started home. But the moment I moved from ‘the devil’s seat,’ the round opening disappeared. However I turned, I could not catch sight of it again. To me, the cleverest part of the whole arrangement is this: the only reachable place from which that circular gap can be seen is the narrow ledge on the face of the rock. I have tested this repeatedly and am certain it is true.

“Jupiter came with me on that visit to the ‘Bishop’s Hotel.’ He had undoubtedly noticed how distracted I had been over the previous few weeks, and was especially careful not to leave me alone. The following morning, however, I got up very early and managed to slip away from him. I went into the hills to look for the tree. After a great deal of effort I found it. When I returned that night, my servant proposed to give me a beating. I believe you know the rest of the adventure as well as I do.”

“I suppose,” I said, “that you dug in the wrong place at first because Jupiter foolishly dropped the bug through the skull’s right eye instead of its left.”

“Exactly. His mistake shifted ‘the shot’—that is, the position of the peg nearest the tree—by about two and a half inches. If the treasure had been buried directly under ‘the shot,’ the mistake would scarcely have mattered. But ‘the shot’ and the nearest point of the trunk were simply two points used to set the direction of a line. Naturally, though the error was tiny at the start, its effect grew as we followed that line farther. By the time we had gone fifty feet, it had led us completely off course.

Despite all this, the boy grew sadder, paler, and more miserable. She added hot baths, sitting baths, showers, and plunges into water. He remained as gloomy as a hearse. She supported the water treatments with a meagre diet of oatmeal and plasters that raised blisters. She worked out how much he could hold as if he were a jug, and filled him daily with fake remedies that promised to cure everything.

By now Tom no longer cared what torments she put him through. This indifference deeply alarmed the old lady. Whatever the cost, she must put an end to it. Just then she heard of Pain-killer for the first time and immediately ordered a large supply. She tasted it and felt full of gratitude. It was nothing less than liquid fire. She abandoned the water treatment and all the other remedies, and placed her trust in Pain-killer. She gave Tom a teaspoonful and watched anxiously to see what happened. Her worries vanished at once, and her soul was peaceful again: his “indifference” had disappeared. The boy could not have reacted with more wild enthusiasm if she had lit a fire beneath him.

Tom decided it was time to stir himself. In his brokenhearted state, this sort of existence might be romantic, but it was beginning to offer too little tender feeling and far too much disturbing variety. He considered several ways to escape, then finally decided to pretend he loved Pain-killer. He asked for it so frequently that he became a nuisance. At last his aunt told him to help himself and stop bothering her. Had Sid behaved this way, her pleasure would have been free of doubt. Since it was Tom, however, she secretly kept watch on the bottle. She saw that the medicine really was disappearing, but it never occurred to her that the boy was using it to improve the health of a crack in the sitting-room floor.

One day, while Tom was giving the crack its dose, his aunt’s yellow cat appeared, purring, staring greedily at the teaspoon and begging for a taste. Tom said:

“Don’t ask for it unless you really want it, Peter.”

Peter made it clear that he did.

“You’d better be sure.”

Peter was sure.

“Well, you asked, and I’ll give it to you, because I’m not mean. But if you decide you don’t like it, you’ve only got yourself to blame.”

Peter accepted these terms. Tom forced his mouth open and poured in the Pain-killer. Peter leaped a couple of yards into the air, let out a war cry, and raced round and round the room, crashing into furniture, knocking over flowerpots, and causing havoc everywhere.
